resources.string: High CO₂ often points to insufficient ventilation. When outdoor air is suitable, open a window or bring in fresh air mechanically. Opening a door may help circulation, but fresh air still needs to enter. Pay closer attention when more people are present or windows stay closed.

CO₂ can build up indoors as people breathe and helps indicate ventilation conditions. A sustained rise suggests a need for more fresh air. It does not represent every pollutant or replace a carbon monoxide alarm.
CO₂

These bands describe outdoor air quality. If a CO alarm sounds or you suspect a combustion leak, leave the affected area immediately and seek local emergency help. Do not wait for a rating change or rely only on opening windows.

Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas that can result from incomplete combustion. This rating uses outdoor air quality references and their averaging periods. Acute hazards require a dedicated alarm; do not wait for an air quality rating to rise.

New furniture or renovation materials may keep releasing formaldehyde. If elevated, look for sources and ventilate when outdoor air is suitable. Persistent readings may warrant professional testing. No noticeable smell does not prove levels have fallen.

Formaldehyde is a gas that may be released by panels, furniture, and other materials. Read concentrations over the averaging period required by the selected reference. If elevated, check emission sources and ventilate when outdoor conditions allow.

When air is dry, add moisture as needed. When damp, check bathrooms, drying laundry, or leaks, then consider exhaust ventilation or a dehumidifier. Opening windows may not help if outdoor air is also humid.

Relative humidity is the percentage of water vapor in the air compared with saturation at the same temperature. Dry air may feel uncomfortable, while persistent dampness supports mold growth. Staying within the selected reference range helps balance comfort and moisture control.
Relative humidity

For reading, writing, or crafts, add a light at the task location and adjust it to avoid hand shadows and glare. Light at the device may differ from the desk, so a higher number is not the goal by itself.

Illuminance measures visible light falling on a surface, in lux. Different activities need different levels; brighter is not always better. A single device reading is a scene hint. Check the actual task surface for reading or work.
Light / Illuminance

If sound affects focus or rest, lower the volume, move noisy equipment, or find a quieter spot. Use the sleep scene for guidance when resting, as sound can be more disruptive then.

Noise readings describe sound level at the measurement location. A weighting reflects the ear’s differing sensitivity to frequencies. Effects on rest depend on duration and context; the sleep scene uses stricter boundaries.

When ozone is high, move strenuous outdoor activities such as running or cycling to a lower forecast period, or shorten them. Check outdoor ozone before opening windows; a fresh smell is not a reliable guide.

This is ground-level ozone, not the protective ozone layer high above Earth. It can form when other pollutants react in sunlight. At elevated levels, consult local forecasts to adjust outdoor activity timing and intensity.

Cleaning, movement, or dusty weather can raise PM10. Damp wiping instead of dry sweeping can reduce dust. Check filtration, and limit open windows when outdoor dust is heavy.

PM10 is inhalable particulate matter generally no more than 10 micrometers in aerodynamic diameter, including PM2.5. Dust, roads, and construction can raise readings. Consider outdoor conditions when controlling dust and improving filtration.

If readings rise after cooking, incense, or smoking, reduce the smoke source, use an extractor, or run particle filtration. Check outdoor air before opening windows; polluted air can bring more particles inside.

PM2.5 is fine airborne particulate matter generally no more than 2.5 micrometers in aerodynamic diameter. Sources include combustion, cooking, and outdoor pollution. These particles can enter the lungs; consider concentration, duration, and outdoor conditions when reducing sources or filtering air.

If you feel cold or warm, try a small change to clothing, air conditioning, or a fan, then give it time. Comfort varies, so there is no need to keep adjusting just to reach Neutral.

PMV estimates a group’s average thermal sensation from air and radiant temperature, humidity, air speed, activity, and clothing. Negative values indicate cooler sensations, positive values warmer ones, and values near zero neutral sensations. Individual feelings can still differ.
PMV thermal sensation

If you are sensitive to pollen, read the count alongside your own reactions. When pollen is abundant, avoid leaving windows open for long and change outer clothing after going out. Different pollen types can affect you differently at the same count.

Pollen readings count grains per volume of air. Allergenic potential and rating thresholds differ by type and reference. Sensitive people can plan activities based on their own response. A total count without a type does not establish a load rating.
Pollen

When outdoor SO₂ is high, spend less time in affected places and move outdoor activities to a cleaner-air period. Consider outdoor readings before ventilating; opening windows may not help when levels are high.

Sulfur dioxide is mainly associated with sulfur-containing fuel combustion and some industrial emissions, and can affect breathing. Interpret readings over the selected reference’s averaging period. At elevated levels, follow local guidance to reduce exposure.

ASHRAE Standard 55’s seven-point thermal sensation scale describes Cold through Neutral to Hot, from −3 to +3. The project uses these names to make PMV easier to understand. Its continuous display bands are product rules; a label alone does not establish compliance with the full standard.
ASHRAE Standard 55 seven-point scale
American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE)
American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE)

The European Environment Agency’s Air Quality Index describes short-term pollution in six levels. It is the default for PM2.5 and PM10, with ozone and sulfur dioxide bands also available. Results describe individual pollutants, rather than a complete official European aggregate index.
EEA European Air Quality Index
European Environment Agency (EEA)
European Environment Agency (EEA)

The US EPA AQI reports air quality in six categories to guide pollution awareness and outdoor activities. The project offers its concentration boundaries for supported pollutants as an alternative reference. Averaging periods and numeric processing differ, so ratings may vary between references.
U.S. EPA AQI
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)

The US EPA’s humidity guidance helps households reduce dampness and mold, recommending indoor relative humidity of 30–50% where possible, and below 60%. This optional reference uses Dry, Suitable, Slightly Humid, and Humid messages to guide humidification, ventilation, or dehumidification.
U.S. EPA humidity guidance
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)

GB/T 18883—2022 is China’s indoor air quality standard, covering pollutant limits and test methods. Its formaldehyde limit is 0.08 mg/m³ over one hour. The project offers this optional reference with six product-defined bands; these do not constitute a full compliance test.
State Administration for Market Regulation / Standardization Administration of China
State Administration for Market Regulation
Standardization Administration of China

HJ 633—2026 defines China’s rules for calculating AQI, assigning pollution categories, and reporting results. The project uses its concentration boundaries for particulate matter and supported outdoor gases. Readings must match the required averaging period: hourly and daily averages are not interchangeable.
Ministry of Ecology and Environment of the People\'s Republic of China
Ministry of Ecology and Environment of the People\'s Republic of China

ANSI/IES/ALA RP-11-26 recommends residential lighting by space, activity, and task surface. The project uses selected illuminance levels for messages from ambient lighting to detail work. A reading at one device location does not represent lighting across a desk or an entire room.
ANSI/IES/ALA RP-11-26
Illuminating Engineering Society (IES) / American Lighting Association (ALA)
Illuminating Engineering Society (IES)
American Lighting Association (ALA)

ISO 7730 explains how people experience the thermal environment, considering temperature, humidity, air speed, radiant temperature, clothing, and activity. PMV and PPD estimate a group’s thermal sensation and likely dissatisfaction. The project uses these methods to describe cooler, warmer, or near-neutral conditions.
International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
International Organization for Standardization (ISO)

MeteoSwiss distinguishes pollen types such as birch, grasses, and ragweed, with concentration boundaries reflecting allergenic potential. The project shows daily-average load classes for supported types. These are not a common EU standard or predictions of an individual’s allergic reaction.
MeteoSwiss pollen load classes
Swiss Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology
Swiss Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology

The US National Allergy Bureau monitors pollen concentrations by category, including trees, grasses, and weeds. The project uses daily-average boundaries for Low, Moderate, High, and Very High messages to help daily planning. Unclassified total counts cannot use a single category’s thresholds.
NAB pollen levels
U.S. National Allergy Bureau (NAB)
U.S. National Allergy Bureau (NAB)

California OEHHA’s reference exposure levels support health risk assessment. Its one-hour acute formaldehyde reference is 0.055 mg/m³. The project offers this option with six product-defined bands. It is a California health reference, not a nationwide US legal limit.
California OEHHA 2008
California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)
California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)

The German Environment Agency’s CO₂ guidance uses 1000 and 2000 ppm to divide indoor ventilation conditions into three ranges. The project presents these as Normal, Ventilate, and Increase Ventilation, helping you decide when to open windows or introduce more fresh air.
German UBA 2008 CO₂ guidance
German Environment Agency (UBA)
German Environment Agency (UBA)

The German Environment Agency recommends roughly 40–60% relative humidity year-round to support ventilation and damp prevention at home. This is the project’s default humidity reference: readings below the range are Dry and those above it Humid, helping you decide whether to add or remove moisture.
German UBA humidity guidance
German Environment Agency (UBA)
German Environment Agency (UBA)

The WHO indoor air quality guidelines provide health-based references, including 0.10 mg/m³ over 30 minutes for formaldehyde. This is the project’s default formaldehyde reference. Its six display bands are product rules around that value, not categories prescribed by WHO.
WHO 2010 Guidelines for Indoor Air Quality
World Health Organization (WHO)
World Health Organization (WHO)

The WHO Guidelines for Community Noise address daily life, rest, and sleep using measures such as long-term equivalent sound levels. The project draws on home and sleep references for noise messages. Its four bands for current readings are product rules, not substitutes for full long-term measurements.
WHO Guidelines for Community Noise
World Health Organization (WHO)
World Health Organization (WHO)

The WHO Global Solar UV Index guide uses five exposure levels to explain potential effects on skin and eyes and guide sun protection. The project adopts these levels and WHO’s RGB colors. Check whether readings show the current index or daily maximum; UV Index differs from illuminance.
WHO Global Solar UV Index
World Health Organization (WHO)
World Health Organization (WHO)
If you feel cold or warm, try a small change to clothing, air conditioning, or a fan, then give it time. Comfort varies, so there is no need to keep adjusting just to reach Neutral.

Temperature describes how warm or cold the air is. Humidity, air movement, clothing, and activity also affect how it feels. The project combines these conditions in PMV to describe seven thermal sensations; it does not rate air temperature alone.
Temperature

The TVOC index tracks changes in a sensor’s combined response to volatile organic compounds. It is not the concentration of one pollutant or a direct measure of toxicity or health risk. This project currently displays readings and trends without rating bands.
TVOC Index
Check the UV Index before heading out and prepare a hat, covering clothing, or sunscreen. At higher levels, use shade and limit midday exposure. Cool or cloudy weather does not always mean low UV.

The UV Index describes the potential strength of solar UV damage to skin and eyes, not visible illuminance. Higher values call for greater attention to sun protection and shade. Distinguish a current reading from the daily maximum.
UV Index
